subject: chemistry
question_text: Which of the alkaline earth metal carbonates is thermally the most stable? Why?

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The carbonate named
lines: the most stable of the alkaline earth
A carbonate of this group decomposes
on heating to the oxide and carbon
steps.why: The question asks for one carbonate by name, so the answer opens with barium carbonate. Thermal stability here means the temperature at which the carbonate breaks into the oxide and carbon dioxide, and barium carbonate needs the highest.
common_mistakes: Naming beryllium carbonate or magnesium carbonate. These two are the least stable of the group.
Giving the name and stopping. The question also asks for the reason.
steps.memory_tip: Stability rises down the group, so the last member, barium carbonate, is the most stable.
steps.margin_note: Write the formula BaCO₃ beside the name.

steps.label: The reason
lines: size of the cation increases down
Ba²⁺ is the largest cation of the
group and its polarising power is
low, so it distorts the carbonate ion
only slightly and the C–O bonds in it
steps.why: A carbonate decomposes when the cation pulls electron density away from the carbonate ion and weakens a C–O bond. A large cation with a low charge density does this least, so the carbonate of the largest cation needs the highest temperature to decompose.
common_mistakes: Writing that thermal stability decreases down the group. It increases, which is why BaCO₃ is the most stable.
Giving the order without the reason. The size of the cation is what the reason rests on.
steps.memory_tip: A bigger cation pulls on the carbonate ion less, so the carbonate is more stable.
steps.margin_note: The stability order written out shows the trend in one line.

insider_note: One name and one reason are the whole answer, but the reason has to be the size of the cation, not the mass of the metal.
